lessons.title: Reading and Interpreting Blueprints
lessons.body: A blueprint is the map of the steel piece you will build. In a typical African workshop, you might receive a hand-drawn sketch or a printed drawing. Learn to read three views: front, top, and side. Each line tells you something: thick solid lines are visible edges, dashed lines are hidden edges, and centre lines are dash-dot. Dimensions are usually in millimetres. For example, a bracket might be 150 mm long, 50 mm wide, and 6 mm thick. Look for the title block in the bottom right corner: it shows the part name, material (e.g., mild steel), and scale (1:1, 1:2, or 1:10). If the scale is 1:2, multiply every dimension by 2 to get real size. Check for notes like 'weld all around' or 'grind flush'. Always verify dimensions by adding them up: if a plate has two holes 40 mm from each end and is 200 mm long, the distance between holes is 120 mm. If the drawing is unclear, ask your supervisor before cutting. In many African workshops, blueprints are reused, so check for revisions. A good habit is to sketch the part on a piece of paper or on the steel itself, marking key points. This helps you catch mistakes early. Remember, a misread dimension can waste expensive steel. So take your time, use a ruler and pencil, and double-check every number.

lessons.title: Measuring Tools and Techniques
lessons.body: You need accurate measurements to avoid gaps and misalignment. The basic tools are a steel rule (150 mm or 300 mm), a measuring tape (3 m or 5 m), a try square, a combination square, and a vernier caliper for precise work. In Africa, you can buy these at hardware stores in cities like Lagos, Nairobi, or Johannesburg. Always keep your tape clean and avoid dropping it. When measuring, place the rule's zero mark exactly on the edge. For a 90-degree check, use a try square: press the stock against the edge and see if the blade touches the other side evenly. If light shows, the corner is not square. To measure the inside of a pipe, use a caliper or an inside micrometer. For long distances, use a tape with a helper to hold the end. A common mistake is reading from the 10 mm mark instead of zero; always check. When marking, use a scriber or soapstone, not a pencil, because pencil lines rub off. For repeated measurements, make a story stick: a straight piece of wood or steel with marks for each length. This speeds up work. In hot climates, metal expands, so measure early in the morning if precision matters. Finally, calibrate your tape by comparing it with a known standard, like a steel rule. If it's off by more than 0.5 mm over 1 m, replace it.

lessons.title: Layout for Cutting and Drilling
lessons.body: Layout means drawing the shape and hole positions on the steel before cutting or drilling. Start by cleaning the surface with a wire brush or rag. Use a scriber or soapstone to mark the outline. For cutting, you need a clear line: use a centre punch to mark hole centres, then scribe a circle around it. For a 10 mm hole, mark the centre with a punch, then use a divider set to 5 mm radius to scribe the circle. For straight cuts, use a steel rule and scriber to draw a line, then use a try square to ensure it's perpendicular. Add a cutting allowance: for oxy-fuel cutting, add 2-3 mm; for angle grinder, add 1-2 mm. So if you need a 100 mm plate, mark 102 mm. For drilling, mark the hole centres with a centre punch and a hammer. Use a dot punch for small holes. If you have multiple identical parts, make a template from thin plywood or steel. In African workshops, a common method is to use a chalk line for long cuts on sheets. For example, to cut a 2 m sheet, snap a chalk line, then cut with a grinder. Always double-check dimensions before cutting. After cutting, file the edges to remove burrs. Remember, layout is the most critical step: a mistake here wastes material and time. So measure twice, mark once.

lessons.title: Marking with Soapstone and Scribe
lessons.body: Soapstone and scribe are your main marking tools. Soapstone is a soft stone that leaves a white mark on steel. It's cheap and works well on dark or rusty surfaces. Use it for rough layout, like marking cut lines on a beam. A scribe is a sharp-pointed steel tool that scratches a fine line. Use it for precise work, like hole positions. To use soapstone, rub it on the steel to create a flat edge, then sharpen it to a point with a file. Hold it like a pencil and draw. For scribe, hold it at a slight angle and drag it along a straightedge. You can also use a scriber with a magnet to hold it. In Africa, soapstone is common in markets; a piece costs very little. Always keep your scribe sharp; a dull point gives a wide, inaccurate line. When marking, use a hammer and centre punch to make a small indentation at hole centres. This guides the drill bit. For curves, use a divider or trammel points. A trammel is a beam with two adjustable points; set the distance, then scribe an arc. For large circles, use a piece of string and a nail. After marking, go over the lines with a permanent marker if you need them to last. But remember, soapstone lines can be wiped off, so mark just before cutting. If you're working in bright sun, soapstone may be hard to see; use a scribe or a marker. Always clean the surface before marking to ensure the line is clear.

lessons.title: Templates and Jigs
lessons.body: A template is a pattern you use to mark many identical parts. A jig holds the workpiece and guides the tool. Both save time and ensure accuracy. For example, if you need 50 identical brackets, make a template from 3 mm plywood or aluminium. Trace the shape onto steel, then cut. For drilling, a drill jig is a plate with hardened bushings that guide the drill bit. In African workshops, you can make simple jigs from scrap steel. For a hole jig, weld a piece of flat bar with a hole to a clamp. For cutting, a straight edge clamped to the work acts as a jig for a grinder or torch. To make a template, first make one perfect part, then use it to mark others. Trace around it with a scriber. For holes, use a transfer punch: a punch that fits the hole and has a centre point to mark the mating part. When making a jig, ensure it is rigid and the bushings are replaceable. A common jig is a welding jig to hold parts at 90 degrees. Use angle iron and clamps. Templates and jigs reduce errors and speed up production. They are essential for repetitive work, like making window frames or gates. In many African metal shops, jigs are made from wood or steel, whatever is available. Always check your template after a few uses; it can wear. Store templates flat to prevent warping.

lessons.title: Tolerance and Allowances
lessons.body: Tolerance is the acceptable variation in a dimension. Allowance is the extra material you leave for machining or fitting. For example, if a shaft must fit a hole, you might make the shaft 0.05 mm smaller than the hole. In steel fabrication, tolerances are often Â±1 mm for cut lengths, Â±0.5 mm for hole positions, and Â±2 mm for overall dimensions. But for structural work, tolerances can be larger. Always check the drawing for tolerance notes. If none, use standard: Â±1 mm for machined parts, Â±2 mm for flame-cut parts. Allowance for welding: steel shrinks when welded, so you may need to add 1-2 mm per 100 mm of weld. For example, a 500 mm beam may shrink 5-10 mm after welding. So cut it 510 mm. For bending, allow for springback: overbend by 2-3 degrees. In Africa, where materials may vary, test with a scrap piece. Use a vernier caliper to check your work. If a part is out of tolerance, it may not fit. So measure after cutting and before welding. A good practice is to make a first article and check it. If it's good, continue. If not, adjust. Remember, tolerance is not about being perfect, but about being within acceptable limits. For a gate, a 2 mm gap is fine; for a machine part, 0.1 mm may be required. Know your application.

quiz.q: What does a thick solid line on a blueprint represent?
quiz.explanation: Thick solid lines show visible edges of the part.

quiz.q: If a drawing has a scale of 1:2, what is the real length of a line measured 75 mm on the drawing?
quiz.explanation: Multiply the drawing measurement by the scale factor (2) to get real size.

quiz.q: Which tool is best for checking a 90-degree corner?
quiz.explanation: A try square is designed to check squareness.

quiz.q: What is a story stick used for?
quiz.explanation: A story stick has marks for repeated lengths, saving time.

quiz.q: When measuring with a tape, where should the zero mark be placed?
options: B) At the edge of the material
C) At the end of the tape
quiz.explanation: Always start from zero at the edge for accurate measurement.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a centre punch?
quiz.explanation: A centre punch creates a small indentation to guide the drill.

quiz.q: How much cutting allowance is typically added for oxy-fuel cutting?
quiz.explanation: Oxy-fuel cutting removes more material, so add 2-3 mm.

quiz.q: What is a template used for?
quiz.explanation: A template is a pattern for marking multiple parts.

quiz.q: Which marking tool leaves a white mark on steel?
quiz.explanation: Soapstone is a soft stone that leaves a white mark.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid using a pencil for marking steel?
quiz.explanation: Pencil marks rub off, while scriber or soapstone marks last longer.

quiz.q: What is a trammel used for?
quiz.explanation: A trammel has adjustable points to scribe arcs and circles.

quiz.q: What is the first step before marking steel?
quiz.explanation: A clean surface ensures the mark is visible and accurate.

quiz.q: What is a jig used for?
quiz.explanation: A jig holds the workpiece and guides the tool for accuracy.

quiz.q: What is a transfer punch used for?
options: A) Marking hole centres on mating parts
quiz.explanation: A transfer punch fits into a hole to mark the centre on another part.

quiz.q: Why are jigs and templates useful in African workshops?
options: B) They speed up repetitive work
D) They are only for large factories
quiz.explanation: Jigs and templates reduce errors and save time on repeated tasks.

quiz.q: What does tolerance mean in steel fabrication?
quiz.explanation: Tolerance is the allowed difference from the specified dimension.

quiz.q: What is a typical tolerance for hole positions in general fabrication?
quiz.explanation: Â±0.5 mm is a common tolerance for hole positions.

quiz.q: Why do you need to add allowance for welding?
quiz.explanation: Welding causes shrinkage, so parts may need extra length.

quiz.q: If a 500 mm beam shrinks 1 mm per 100 mm after welding, what should be the cut length?
quiz.explanation: Shrinkage of 5 mm (1 mm per 100 mm) means cut 505 mm to end at 500 mm.

quiz.q: What is springback in bending?
options: A) The metal returns slightly after bending
quiz.explanation: Springback is the elastic recovery of metal after bending.

quiz.q: Which tool is best for precise measurement of a shaft diameter?
quiz.explanation: A vernier caliper measures to 0.02 mm accuracy.

quiz.q: What should you do if a drawing has no tolerance notes?
quiz.explanation: Standard tolerances apply when not specified.

quiz.q: What is a first article inspection?
options: A) Checking the first part made
quiz.explanation: First article inspection verifies the first part before mass production.

quiz.q: Which of these is a common marking tool in African workshops?
quiz.explanation: Soapstone is cheap and widely available.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a centre line on a drawing?
options: B) Indicate symmetry or centre of holes
quiz.explanation: Centre lines indicate axes of symmetry or hole centres.

quiz.q: How can you check if your tape measure is accurate?
options: A) Compare with a steel rule
B) Use it to cut steel
quiz.explanation: Compare with a known standard like a steel rule.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of using a scribe over soapstone?
options: B) It leaves a finer, more precise line
C) It is easier to see
quiz.explanation: A scribe scratches a fine line for precision work.

quiz.q: What is a common allowance for grinding after cutting?
quiz.explanation: Grinding removes about 1-2 mm, so leave that allowance.

quiz.q: Why is it important to double-check dimensions before cutting?
quiz.explanation: A mistake in cutting wastes expensive steel.

quiz.q: What does a dashed line on a blueprint indicate?
quiz.explanation: Dashed lines represent edges that are hidden from view.
